4600:
Imagine you and a friend are walking together. At some point, you reach a fork in the road. You go left, your friend goes right. The further you both walk, the more distance grows between you. That image — two things starting from the same place and moving away from each other — is the heart of what divergent means.

Divergent describes things that are moving apart, separating, or becoming increasingly different from each other or from a common point. It is the opposite of coming together.

The word works in two closely related ways:

1. Moving physically apart from a shared point.
Two roads, rays of light, or river branches that spread outward from a single point are divergent. Think of a flashlight beam that fans out as it travels — the rays are divergent because they keep getting farther apart from each other.

2. Differing in opinion, nature, or direction (non-physically).
Two people can have divergent views on politics. Two countries can follow divergent economic policies. Here, no one is literally walking anywhere — but the idea is the same: they started from a similar place (maybe the same conversation, same culture, same starting point) and have ended up in very different positions.

In both senses, the word stresses the growing gap — the fact that two or more things are not just different, but are pulling away from each other.

Divergent implies direction and movement, not just difference.
"Different" is a still photograph — it just shows two things are unlike. "Divergent" is a video — it shows two things moving apart. So when you say two opinions are divergent, you are saying more than just "they disagree." You are saying their paths of thinking are pulling them further and further from each other.

Divergent often implies a shared origin or reference point.
Things are described as divergent when they were (or could have been) together, but have split. A company's two product lines that once had the same vision but are now going in completely different directions are divergent. Two siblings raised in the same home but who grew up to lead very divergent lives — that contrast is striking precisely because of the shared start.

Divergent can carry a neutral, positive, or slightly tense tone depending on context.
In science, divergent is simply descriptive. In human relationships or politics, calling views "divergent" often signals that agreement or compromise will be difficult, because the gap between the positions keeps widening rather than closing.
How It Is Used in Specific Fields

In everyday language:
You will most commonly hear it describing opinions, paths, goals, strategies, or outcomes that are going in different directions.

"The two candidates held divergent views on immigration."
"Their careers took divergent paths after college."
"The committee members had divergent priorities, which made agreement difficult."

In mathematics:
A divergent series or sequence is one that does not settle toward a fixed, finite value — it keeps growing or fluctuating without limit. It is the opposite of a convergent series, which homes in on a specific number. For example, adding 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... forever gives you a divergent sum — it has no finite destination, it just keeps growing.

In science and biology:
Divergent evolution describes the process where two species that once shared a common ancestor gradually develop very different characteristics over time because they adapted to different environments. Dogs and wolves share an ancestor, but their traits have become increasingly divergent over thousands of years.

In physics and optics:
Light rays or beams that spread outward away from a source — like the beam from a torch spreading wider as it travels — are divergent. A divergent lens causes parallel rays of light to spread apart.

The natural pair and opposite of divergent is convergent — which describes things coming together, meeting at a point, or moving toward agreement. Understanding this contrast sharpens the meaning of both words.

Divergent → spreading apart, moving away, increasing difference.
Convergent → coming together, narrowing in, approaching a common point.

Two rivers that merge into one are convergent. Two friends whose opinions slowly come closer through conversation are moving in a convergent direction.
Common Word Pairings You Will See

• divergent views / opinions / perspectives — people who think very differently from each other
  • divergent paths / routes / trajectories — directions in life, career, or physical space that split apart
  • divergent goals / interests / priorities — what different people or groups want, pulling in different directions
  • divergent evolution — species branching apart over time
  • divergent series — a mathematical sequence without a finite limit
  • divergent thinking — a style of creative thinking that explores many different directions and possibilities simultaneously, instead of narrowing down to one answer (the opposite of convergent thinking, which focuses on finding the single correct answer)

If two friends start a business together with the same dream, but over five years one wants to expand globally and the other wants to keep it small and local — their visions have become divergent. They began at the same point, but their ideas are now pulling in opposite directions, and the gap is growing.

That growing gap, that spreading apart, that pull in different directions — that is divergent in its full, complete sense.
4601: Diverse means made up of many different kinds of people, things, or ideas — not just one kind, or types that are all very similar to each other. When a group is diverse, it contains rich, meaningful variety among its members.
The Simplest Way to Picture It

Imagine two gardens. The first has only red roses — hundreds of them, all the same plant. The second has roses, sunflowers, orchids, ferns, tulips, and dozens of other plants in many colors and shapes. The second garden is diverse. The first is not — it is uniform.

That single contrast captures everything: diverse = great, meaningful variety within a group.

Two things must be true for something to be called diverse.

First, you need a collection — a group of things, people, or ideas, not a single item by itself. You cannot describe one apple as diverse. But a fruit basket filled with apples, mangoes, grapes, papayas, and kiwis? That is diverse.

Second, the variety must be meaningful and noticeable — not just tiny, barely visible differences. A bag of a thousand sand grains is not diverse even though no two grains are perfectly identical, because the differences are insignificant. But a bag containing sand, pebbles, shells, and soil would be diverse because the differences are real and clearly visible.

Diversity comes in degrees. A classroom with students from five countries is somewhat diverse. A classroom with students from forty countries, speaking thirty languages, with vastly different life experiences, is highly diverse. This is why you will often see "diverse" used alongside words like very, highly, incredibly, remarkably, or fairly. You can also compare: "This city is more diverse than that one."
Where You Will Encounter This Word

Diverse is a very widely used word that appears across many areas of life.

People and Society. This is the most common context. A "diverse workforce" is one where employees come from many different racial, ethnic, cultural, national, religious, and gender backgrounds. A "diverse community" is one where people of many different identities and origins live together. A "diverse school" has students from many different walks of life. When people say "we need more diversity," they are asking for the group to become more diverse — to include a wider range of people.

Nature and Science. A tropical rainforest is one of the most diverse ecosystems on Earth, because it is home to an extraordinary range of plants, animals, insects, and fungi. A barren desert with very few species is far less diverse. In biology, scientists talk about "species diversity" to describe how many different types of living things exist in a particular environment.

Ideas and Perspectives. A "diverse range of opinions" means that many different viewpoints exist — not just one dominant position. When a panel of speakers holds diverse perspectives, they each bring genuinely different ways of seeing the same issue. This is considered valuable because it prevents narrow thinking.

Skills and Abilities. We say someone has a "diverse skill set" if they are capable in many very different areas — for example, a person who can write poetry, fix a car engine, speak four languages, and manage a team all at once. Their abilities are not clustered in one area; they span many different domains.

Everyday Things. You might also read about "a diverse range of products" (a store selling many different types of items), "diverse reading material" (books covering many different topics and genres), or "diverse investment portfolio" (money spread across many different types of assets).
Common Phrases You Will Regularly See

Diverse is reliably paired with certain nouns. Knowing these combinations will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

Diverse backgrounds, diverse perspectives, diverse range, diverse group, diverse workforce, diverse community, diverse ecosystem, diverse skill set, culturally diverse, diverse set of experiences.

In every single one of these phrases, the core idea is the same: a collection that contains many genuinely different kinds.
What "Diverse" Does NOT Mean — Important Distinctions

Diverse is sometimes confused with the word different, but they are not the same. "Different" simply describes the relationship between two specific things — "these two jackets are different" just means they are not identical. Diverse, by contrast, describes a whole group and the richness of variety within it. It is a word about a collection, not a comparison between two items.

Diverse also does not mean "random" or "unrelated." A diverse group is not just a chaotic jumble — it is a group that contains meaningful variety, even if the members share an overall common purpose or identity.
Similar Words (Synonyms) and How They Differ

Several words are close in meaning to diverse, but each has its own slightly different feel.

Varied is the closest everyday synonym. It also means having many different types or kinds. However, "varied" is a bit more neutral and lighter in tone. A "varied menu" simply means the menu has several options. "Diverse" implies a broader, richer, more significant range of difference — it carries a slightly stronger weight.

Assorted usually refers to a mix of different kinds of physical items — "an assorted box of chocolates" or "assorted biscuits." It is almost never used for people or ideas, and it feels more casual and commercial.

Heterogeneous is a formal, technical word used mostly in science and academic writing. It means made up of different or dissimilar elements. It carries exactly the same core idea as diverse, but sounds clinical and is rarely used in everyday speech.

Mixed means combining different types, but it tends to be vaguer and more casual. "A mixed group of students" tells you much less than "a diverse group of students."

The opposite of diverse is any word that describes a group where everything is the same type or very similar.

Uniform means all the same, without variation. A uniform group has no meaningful differences among its members.

Homogeneous means made of the same or very similar elements throughout. A homogeneous community is one where all members share the same background, culture, and identity — the polar opposite of a diverse one.

Identical means exactly the same in every way — the furthest possible point from diverse.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Diverse = rich in variety. Whenever a group of people, a collection of things, or a set of ideas contains many genuinely different kinds of members or elements, it is diverse. The more different types it contains — and the more meaningfully different they are from one another — the more diverse it is. Its opposite is a group where everything is the same, which we call uniform or homogeneous.

The next time you see the word "diverse," ask yourself: Is this a group? Does it contain many genuinely different types? If yes to both — that is diverse.
4602: A diversion means turning something away from where it was originally headed. Think of a river that normally flows straight, but someone builds a wall and forces the water to flow in a different direction. That act — and the new path — is a diversion. Everything else this word means flows from that same idea: something gets redirected.

1. Rerouting Something Along a Different Path

This is the most literal meaning. When a road, route, or flow of something is redirected away from its usual path, that redirect is called a diversion.

Examples:

  • "There's a diversion ahead — the main road is closed, so follow the signs for the alternate route."
  • "The diversion of the river caused flooding in the neighboring town."
  • "Investigators discovered the diversion of company funds into a private account." (Here, money was redirected away from where it was supposed to go — often used when the act is illegal or improper.)

Notice how in all these cases, something — traffic, water, or money — was supposed to go one way but was sent another way instead.

2. A Deliberate Distraction

This is perhaps the most exciting meaning. A diversion is something done on purpose to pull someone's attention away, so that something else can happen without being noticed. You're not redirecting a road here — you're redirecting someone's focus.

Examples:

  • "One thief created a diversion by dropping a bag of groceries, while the other slipped out of the store unnoticed."
  • "The army launched a small attack on the left side as a diversion, while the real assault came from the right."
  • "He started an argument in the hallway as a diversion so his friends could set up the surprise party."

The key here is intent. A diversion in this sense is always planned. Someone is deliberately pulling your attention in the wrong direction. Magicians do this constantly — the flashy movement of one hand is the diversion while the other hand does the real trick.

3. An Activity That Gives You Pleasure and Rest (Entertainment / Leisure)

This meaning is a little softer and more personal. A diversion here is something enjoyable that you turn to in order to take a break from serious matters — it "diverts" your mind away from stress, work, or boredom.

Examples:

  • "After a long week of work, painting is his favorite diversion."
  • "The long train journey was made bearable by a few pleasant diversions — good music and an entertaining book."
  • "The king sought diversion in hunting and banquets."

Think of it this way: your mind is constantly occupied with responsibilities and worries. A diversion gives it somewhere else pleasant to go, even if only temporarily. This meaning is common in formal writing and literature, but you'll still hear it in everyday speech.
How the Three Meanings Are Connected

It helps to see all three meanings as versions of the same idea:

  • In meaning 1, a route or flow is turned away from its path.
  • In meaning 2, a person's attention is turned away from what's really happening.
  • In meaning 3, a person's mind is turned away from stress or seriousness toward something enjoyable.

The common thread is always: something is redirected away from one thing and toward another.

"Diversion" vs. "distraction": These can feel similar, but there's a difference in tone. A distraction is usually accidental or unwanted ("Sorry, I was distracted"). A diversion — especially in meanings 2 and 3 — tends to be more deliberate and purposeful. A magician creates a diversion, not a distraction.

"Diversion" in law and justice: You may encounter phrases like diversion program or pretrial diversion. This refers to a legal process where a person accused of a minor crime is redirected away from the traditional court system and toward counseling, community service, or rehabilitation instead. It's still the same idea — the case is rerouted.

Plural — "diversions": The word works perfectly in plural form. "The city offered many diversions for tourists." "Military diversions were planned on multiple fronts."

Read these three sentences and see if you can identify which meaning is being used:

  • "The flooding was caused by an illegal diversion of the stream." → Meaning 1 — physical rerouting
  • "She knocked over the vase as a diversion while her brother hid the gift." → Meaning 2 — deliberate distraction
  • "Chess has been his favorite diversion since childhood." → Meaning 3 — pleasurable pastime

In short, diversion always carries the idea of something being turned away — whether it's a road, someone's attention, or a restless mind seeking pleasure. Once you see that unifying thread, the word becomes very easy to use and recognize across all contexts.
4603:
Diversity means the presence of many different types, kinds, or varieties of things existing together in the same place, group, or system.

Think of a forest. If it has only one type of tree, it has low diversity. But if it has hundreds of different trees, plants, animals, and insects all living together, it has high diversity. The more different kinds of things there are, the more diversity there is.

The single most important idea at the heart of the word is this: variety within a group.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine a bag of marbles. If every marble is red, there is no diversity — everything is the same. But if the bag contains red, blue, green, yellow, and purple marbles, the bag has diversity. The differences among those marbles, all present in the same bag, is the diversity.

Now replace marbles with people, animals, ideas, or anything else — the concept works the same way.

Diversity is not limited to one subject. It applies broadly across many areas of life:

People and Society
This is the most common use today. A society, school, team, or organisation has diversity when its members come from different backgrounds and carry different characteristics. This includes differences in:

  • Race and ethnicity
  • Gender and age
  • Religion and beliefs
  • Language and nationality
  • Economic background
  • Education level
  • Sexual orientation
  • Physical ability or disability

When people talk about "diversity" in workplaces or schools, this is almost always what they mean — a mix of people with different life experiences and identities.

Culture
Cultural diversity refers to the existence of many different cultures, traditions, customs, and ways of life within a region or the world. A city where people celebrate different festivals, eat different foods, and speak different languages has high cultural diversity.

Nature and Biology
In science, diversity refers to the variety of living things. A jungle with thousands of species of animals, insects, and plants has enormous biological diversity (commonly called biodiversity). This is critically important for the health of ecosystems — a forest with only one species of tree is far more vulnerable to disease than one with many species.

Genetic diversity refers to the variation in genes within a single species. A population where individuals have very similar genes has low genetic diversity, making it fragile. Greater genetic variation makes a species more adaptable and resilient.

Ideas and Opinions
Diversity of thought means a range of different perspectives, viewpoints, and ways of thinking. A team that has diversity of thought approaches problems from many angles, which usually leads to better, more creative solutions than a team where everyone thinks the same way.

Skills and Expertise
A team can have a diversity of skills — meaning different members bring different abilities, knowledge, and strengths. One person is good at analysis, another at communication, another at design, and so on.

1. It is about differences, not just numbers.
Having 100 people is not diversity. Having 100 people who all come from the same background, think the same way, and look the same is uniformity. Diversity requires that those people differ from one another in meaningful ways.

2. It requires coexistence.
The different things must be present together — in the same space, group, or system. Ten different species living on separate islands is not biodiversity in one ecosystem. Ten different species sharing the same forest is.

3. It exists on a spectrum.
Diversity is not simply "present" or "absent" — it exists in degrees. A group can have a little diversity or a great deal of it. You can always ask: how diverse is this? More variety = more diversity.

4. It is neutral as a description.
The word "diversity" by itself simply describes a fact — the presence of variety. It does not automatically mean "good" or "bad." However, in most modern usage — especially in social, workplace, and environmental contexts — diversity is viewed positively, because variety tends to bring strength, resilience, and richness.

Variety is a close synonym, but "variety" is lighter and more casual. You might say a menu has a "variety" of dishes. "Diversity" carries more weight — it usually implies a broader, more significant, or more meaningful range of differences. You would not normally say a menu has "diversity" unless you were making a specific point about its cultural range.

Heterogeneity is the formal, scientific word for diversity — it means "composed of different kinds." Its opposite, homogeneity, means "composed of the same kind." In everyday language, diversity is preferred.

Multiculturalism is a specific type of diversity — it refers only to cultural and ethnic diversity and often implies a social or political attitude of welcoming that diversity.

Inclusion is a related but different concept. Diversity describes who is present. Inclusion describes how those people are treated — whether they feel welcomed, valued, and able to participate fully. Diversity without inclusion means you have a mix of people but some of them are ignored or marginalised. The two concepts are often discussed together, especially in workplaces.

Plurality means having more than one type or more than one element, but it does not imply a wide range. A group could have plurality (more than one kind of person) but still have very low diversity.

• "Diversity of opinion" — a range of different views on a topic.
  • "Diversity and inclusion" (D&I) — a common phrase in workplaces referring to efforts to have a varied workforce and ensure everyone feels equally respected and included.
  • "Celebrate diversity" — to welcome and appreciate differences rather than merely tolerate them.
  • "Lack of diversity" — when a group is too uniform; when there is not enough variety.
  • "Diversity of species" — the number of different animal or plant species in an area.
  • "A diversity of approaches" — several different methods or strategies being used.

The opposite of diversity is:

  • Uniformity — everything being identical or the same.
  • Homogeneity — being composed of all the same kind.
  • Monotony — (in a looser sense) dull sameness, with no variation.

Understanding why diversity is considered valuable helps deepen your understanding of the word:

  • In nature, diverse ecosystems are more resilient. If one species disappears, others can fill its role. A forest with only one tree species can be wiped out by a single disease.
  • In organisations and teams, diversity of backgrounds and thought tends to produce more creative ideas, catch more errors, and solve problems more effectively, because different people notice different things.
  • In culture and society, diversity allows different traditions, languages, and ways of life to survive and enrich one another.
  • In genetics, diverse populations are better equipped to adapt to changing environments.

Diversity is the noun that names the state of having a wide variety of different types of things coexisting within a group or system. The more different kinds there are, and the more meaningfully they differ, the greater the diversity. It applies to people, cultures, species, ideas, genes, skills — almost anything where variety can exist. In common modern usage, especially in social and professional life, it most often refers to the range of different human backgrounds and identities within a group, and it is generally seen as a strength.
4604:
Divert means to deliberately turn something — or someone — away from its original path and send it in a new direction.

Picture a river flowing steadily toward the sea. Now imagine engineers building a channel that forces the water to change course and flow into a reservoir instead. That act of making it change course is diverting it.

This one idea — redirecting something from its original path — runs through every single use of the word.

1. To physically redirect something that is moving

This is the most literal sense. When something is on its way from A to B, and you make it go to C instead, you divert it.

  • "Bad weather forced the pilot to divert the flight to a nearby airport." (The plane was heading to one city; it was sent to another.)
  • "Police diverted traffic away from the accident scene." (Cars were sent along a different route.)
  • "Engineers diverted the river to prevent flooding." (The water's natural path was changed.)

Notice something important: the thing being diverted doesn't just stop — it goes somewhere else. Divert always involves a new destination, not just a pause.

2. To redirect attention, focus, or suspicion

You can divert things that aren't physical either — like a person's attention or suspicion. This means deliberately steering someone's mental focus away from one thing and toward another.

  • "The politician diverted attention from the scandal by announcing a new policy."
  • "She diverted his suspicion by acting completely calm."
  • "The magician diverted the audience's attention while switching the cards."

This is worth distinguishing from a similar word: distract often implies an accidental or unwanted break in focus ("The loud music distracted me"). Divert, on the other hand, almost always implies a deliberate, strategic redirection — someone is purposefully steering the attention elsewhere.

3. To redirect money, resources, or effort

When money, funds, or effort that were meant for one purpose are redirected to a completely different purpose, we say they were diverted.

  • "He was accused of diverting company funds into his personal account."
  • "The government diverted money from healthcare to build roads."
  • "After her promotion, she diverted more of her energy toward leadership."

The first two examples carry a negative, often wrongful tone — "diverting funds" in a business or legal context almost always implies misuse. The third is neutral, simply describing a personal shift in priorities. So pay close attention to context: the same verb can be neutral or accusatory depending on the situation.

4. To entertain or amuse someone

This meaning is older and less common in everyday speech today, but you will still encounter it in literature and more formal writing. To divert someone here means to give their mind a pleasant detour — away from boredom, worry, or routine.

  • "The comedian diverted the crowd with clever stories."
  • "She read novels to divert herself during her long recovery."

This is exactly where the word diversion gets its common meaning of "a fun or relaxing activity" — as in, "Cooking is my favorite diversion." The mind is being temporarily redirected somewhere pleasant. Same core idea, just applied to amusement.
The Thread That Connects All Four Meanings

Look at them together:

  • Redirecting a plane → changing its physical direction
  • Redirecting attention → changing someone's mental focus
  • Redirecting money → changing where resources flow
  • Entertaining someone → giving the mind a pleasant detour

In every case, something that was going in one direction is now going in another. Divert always implies a deliberate change of course. Nothing wanders off by accident — something or someone actively causes the redirection.

Divert almost always needs an object — you divert something or someone. It rarely appears alone.

Common patterns you'll encounter:

  • divert + [a thing] → divert traffic, divert funds, divert a river, divert a flight
  • divert + [someone's attention/suspicion] → divert her attention, divert public suspicion
  • divert + [someone] + from + [something] → divert him from his original plan, divert her from the truth
  • divert + [someone] (to entertain) → divert the children, divert the audience
Words That Are Close — But Not the Same

Redirect is the closest word to divert and the two are often interchangeable. However, redirect is more neutral and clean ("redirect the call"), while divert carries a stronger sense of pulling something away from its intended path — sometimes suggesting effort or even interference.

Deflect means to make something bounce off in a new direction — it's commonly used for criticism or blame ("He deflected the question"). It's more about bouncing something away than steering it somewhere specific.

Distract means to accidentally break someone's focus. Divert is almost always more purposeful and strategic than distract.

Divert = to deliberately turn something (a vehicle, water, money, attention, or a person's mind) away from where it was originally going, and send it somewhere else.

Whether you are reading about a detoured flight, diverted river, misused funds, a magician's trick, or someone reading a novel for pleasure — the verb divert is doing exactly the same job every time: making something change course.
4605:
If something is diverting, it is pleasantly entertaining or amusing — it captures your attention in a light, enjoyable way and gives you a welcome break from boredom, routine, or serious matters.

Think of it as something that is fun to engage with, not in a thrilling or intense way, but in a calm, pleasant, "I'm enjoying this" kind of way.
The core feeling behind the word

Imagine you've had a long, tiring day. You pick up a clever little novel, and before you know it, an hour has passed and you've been smiling the whole time. That novel is diverting. It didn't shake your world. It didn't make you cry or keep you up at night in deep thought. It simply kept you happily occupied and took your mind off everything else.

That pleasant, light, attention-holding quality — that is what "diverting" captures.
What makes it different from similar words

"Diverting" sits in a specific zone among words like entertaining, amusing, fun, and interesting. Here's how to understand where it fits:

  • Entertaining is the broadest word — anything enjoyable falls here.
  • Amusing leans toward something that makes you smile or lightly laugh.
  • Fun is casual and energetic.
  • Diverting is more refined and gentle. It suggests something that pleasantly occupies your mind without demanding too much from you. It has a slightly formal, old-fashioned flavour — you're more likely to read it in a book or hear it from an educated speaker than in everyday casual conversation.

The key idea inside "diverting" is that something turns your attention away from dullness or worry and keeps it pleasantly engaged. It doesn't overwhelm you — it simply holds you in a light, agreeable way.

"Diverting" is a mild-to-moderate positive. It is a compliment, but not a strong one. If you call a film "diverting," you're saying it was enjoyable and held your attention — but you're not saying it was brilliant, powerful, or unforgettable. It's the kind of word you might use when something was better than you expected but you wouldn't necessarily rush to recommend it to everyone.

Think of a scale:

Tolerable → Diverting → Enjoyable → Entertaining → Captivating → Brilliant

It sits comfortably in the lighter, pleasant end of that range.

This is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are unlikely to hear someone casually say "That pizza was diverting!" — that would sound odd. It is most naturally used to describe:

  • Books, plays, films, or shows
  • Conversations or anecdotes
  • Activities or outings
  • Performances

It carries a sense of refinement and mild understatement — the kind of word a thoughtful person might use when they want to say something was pleasant without being over-the-top about it.

• "The afternoon lecture was surprisingly diverting — I hadn't expected to enjoy it so much."
  • "She passed the long train journey with a diverting little mystery novel."
  • "His diverting anecdotes kept the dinner table lively all evening."
  • "The comedy was not a masterpiece, but it was perfectly diverting for a rainy Sunday."
  • "I found the documentary quite diverting, though it didn't tell me anything I hadn't already known."

Avoid using "diverting" for things that are:

  • Deeply moving or powerful — a heart-wrenching drama is not "diverting"; it's something stronger.
  • Intensely exciting — a white-knuckle thriller is not "diverting"; it's gripping or riveting.
  • Trivial or boring — "diverting" is a positive word; it should not be used for something dull.
  • Non-entertainment contexts — you wouldn't call a scientific discovery or a business report "diverting" (unless you're being deliberately witty or ironic).

Diverting means pleasantly entertaining in a light, agreeable way — something that holds your attention and amuses you without being deeply intense or profoundly significant.

Master that idea, and you've mastered the word.
4606:
Divest means to deliberately remove, strip away, or get rid of something — whether that something is money, power, property, or even an abstract thing like responsibility. It always involves a conscious decision to separate yourself (or someone else) from something you currently hold or possess.

Think of it as the opposite of holding on. When you divest, you let go — intentionally and with purpose.

1. The Financial Meaning (the most common use today)

In business and finance, to divest means to sell off an asset, investment, or part of a business. A person, company, or institution divests when they decide to sell something they own — stocks, property, a subsidiary company, or an entire business division.

Why would someone divest?

  • Strategic reasons: A company might divest a department that no longer fits its core business. (e.g., a tech company selling off its hardware division to focus on software.)
  • Financial reasons: An investor might divest shares to raise cash or cut losses.
  • Ethical or political reasons: An institution like a university might divest from companies it finds morally objectionable — such as weapons manufacturers or fossil fuel companies. This kind of organized, values-driven divestment is called a divestment campaign.
  • Legal/regulatory reasons: A government might force a large company to divest some of its businesses to prevent a monopoly.

Examples:

  • "Under pressure from shareholders, the company divested its coal assets."
  • "She decided to divest her stocks before the market crashed."
  • "The university was urged to divest from tobacco companies."
  • "The merger was approved only after the firm agreed to divest three of its brands."

Quick contrast: If invest means to put money into something, then divest is the reverse — to pull out by selling. They are financial opposites.

2. The General Meaning — To Strip or Deprive of Something

In a broader, more formal sense, divest means to take away or remove something from someone — usually something significant like power, authority, rights, a title, or property. It can also mean to rid oneself of something.

This meaning is often used in formal writing, law, politics, and literature.

Examples (stripping someone else):

  • "The court divested him of all parental rights."
  • "The coup divested the president of her authority overnight."
  • "He was divested of his military rank following the tribunal."

Examples (ridding oneself — the reflexive use):
This is the phrase "divest oneself of" — meaning to deliberately shed or free yourself from something.

  • "She divested herself of her coat and sat down." (literal — removing clothing)
  • "He tried to divest himself of any blame for the project's failure." (abstract — shedding responsibility)
  • "Writing in her journal helped her divest herself of years of bottled-up grief." (shedding an emotional burden)

This deserves special attention because it appears frequently. "To divest oneself of something" means to deliberately rid yourself of it — to consciously shed, remove, or free yourself from it.

It can apply to:

  • Physical things: clothing, weapons, belongings
  • Abstract things: responsibility, guilt, identity, biases, habits
  • Power or roles: someone voluntarily giving up authority or a position

The key idea is always intentionality — you are actively choosing to separate yourself from that thing.

• "Divest of" → used when someone is stripped by an outside force: "He was divested of his title."
  • "Divest from" → common in finance: "The pension fund divested from arms manufacturers."
  • "Divest oneself of" → used when you are the one doing the removing: "She divested herself of all luxury."

Knowing the noun forms will help you recognize the word in the wild:

  • Divestment — the act of divesting, especially in ethical/political contexts. "The divestment movement urged colleges to pull funds from fossil fuels."
  • Divestiture — more commonly used in business and legal contexts, referring to the formal sale of assets or a business division. "The regulatory body required full divestiture of the subsidiary."
A Note on Tone and Register

"Divest" is a formal word. You will see it in:

  • Financial news and business reports
  • Legal documents and court rulings
  • Political and activist writing
  • Academic and formal essays

In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "sell off," "get rid of," "strip of," or "shed" — but "divest" carries more weight and precision in formal contexts.

ContextWhat it meansSimple substitute
Finance/BusinessSell off assets or investments"sell off"
CorporateBreak off and sell a part of a company"spin off", "sell off"
Power/AuthorityTake away someone's power or rights"strip of"
Reflexive (oneself)Deliberately shed or free yourself from something"rid yourself of", "shed"

In short: divest = to deliberately remove, sell off, or strip away — whether it's money and assets (financial sense) or power, rights, and burdens (general sense). The common thread across all uses is intentional separation from something you currently hold.
4607:
Divide means to take something whole and break it into two or more separate parts. Think of it as drawing a line — real or imaginary — through something so that what was one becomes many.

The key insight: dividing always creates a distinction, a boundary, or a separation. Whatever is on one side is no longer the same as what is on the other.

1. To cut or split something into parts

This is the most literal use. You take something and separate it into pieces.

  • She divided the orange into four segments.
  • The chef divided the dough into small balls.
  • Divide the paper in half.

The parts don't have to be equal. You just separate a whole into portions.

2. To separate people or things into groups

You don't physically cut anything here — you sort or organize.

  • The teacher divided the students into teams.
  • Let's divide the tasks between us so we finish faster.
  • He divided the books into fiction and non-fiction.

Notice that something that existed as a single collection is now split into distinct groups.

3. To act as a boundary between two things

Here, something is the dividing line. It stands between two areas or things, keeping them apart.

  • A tall fence divides the two properties.
  • The river divides the city into east and west.
  • The mountain range divides the two countries.

The subject (the fence, the river) doesn't move — it simply sits there as the separator.

4. To share or distribute something among people

When you divide something among people, you are giving each person a portion of it.

  • They divided the prize money equally among the winners.
  • After their father passed away, the children divided his belongings.
  • Divide the remaining food between the two of you.

This sense is close to "share out." The whole thing gets distributed so that different people receive different parts of it.

5. To split your time or attention between things

You can divide something intangible too — like your time, focus, or loyalty.

  • She divides her time between her job and her studies.
  • His attention was divided between the movie and his phone.
  • The soldier divided his loyalty between his country and his family.

This means a part of your time/attention goes here, and another part goes there — nothing is given fully to just one thing.

6. To cause disagreement or conflict (between people or groups)

This is a powerful and important use. When an issue or topic divides people, it creates opposing sides — some people believe one thing, others believe the opposite, and they become split from each other emotionally, politically, or ideologically.

  • The new law deeply divided the nation.
  • The debate over religion has divided families for centuries.
  • That one decision divided the whole team.

Notice that no physical cutting happens here. People are "divided" in the sense that they now stand on opposite sides of an issue.

7. In mathematics — to perform division

When you divide one number by another, you are finding out how many times the second number fits into the first.

  • Divide 20 by 4, and you get 5.
  • If you divide 9 by 3, the answer is 3.
  • She divided 100 equally among 5 people, so each got 20.

The word "by" is key here: divide X by Y.

8. To separate or distinguish one thing from another (abstract)

You can also "divide" concepts, ideas, or categories — not physically, but intellectually — to distinguish between them.

  • It is sometimes difficult to divide fact from fiction.
  • Good science divides what we know from what we merely believe.
  • The line that divides bravery from recklessness is thin.

Here, divide means to draw a clear distinction — to say "this is one thing, and that is a different thing."
How "Divide" Works in a Sentence — Key Patterns

The word divide naturally pairs with certain prepositions, and each pairing has its own meaning:

  • divide into → split into parts or groups
    Divide the class into two groups.*
  • divide among → share among three or more people
    Divide the cake among the six children.*
  • divide between → share between two people or things
    Divide the work between the two of you.*
  • divide by → mathematical division
    Divide 50 by 10.*
  • divide from → separate or distinguish one thing from another
    Divide the real information from the noise.*

When you say "divide among" vs "divide between" — traditionally, between is used for two things/people, and among is used for three or more. In practice, many fluent speakers use them interchangeably, but knowing the distinction is useful for precise writing.

  • Divide the candy between the two kids. (two people)
  • Divide the candy among the five kids. (more than two)
The Idea of Something Dividing on Its Own

"Divide" can also be used without an object — meaning something splits or branches by itself (no one is doing the dividing):

  • The road divides just past the river — take the left fork.
  • At this point, the river divides into two streams.
  • The cells divide and multiply.

In biology, "cells divide" means one cell splits into two on its own — a fundamental process of life.
What Makes "Divide" Different from Similar Words

Several words are close to "divide" but not identical:

  • Split — more sudden, often implies force or breaking apart. The wood split in two. More informal.
  • Separate — broader; means to move things apart that were together, but doesn't necessarily create equal or defined parts. Separate the good fruit from the bad.
  • Partition — to divide something into formally defined sections, often with a barrier or boundary. The country was partitioned after the war. More formal, more permanent.
  • Segment — to cut into segments, often equal, often circular (like a pie). More specific.
  • Distribute — to give out portions; overlaps with the "sharing" sense of divide but doesn't emphasize creating parts from a whole.

Divide is the most versatile of these. It covers physical splitting, sharing, creating boundaries, causing conflict, and mathematical operations — all under one word.

No matter which meaning you use, divide always comes back to one fundamental idea: one thing becoming more than one. A line is drawn — physical, social, mathematical, or conceptual — and what was unified is now in parts. That is the soul of the word.
4608: The word dividend has two main meanings — one in everyday finance and investing, and one in mathematics. There is also a looser figurative use.
1. The Financial Meaning (the most common one)

The core idea

When a company earns a profit, its leaders have a choice: they can put that money back into the business (to grow it, buy equipment, hire people, etc.), or they can share some of that profit directly with the people who own the company. Those owners are called shareholders — people who have purchased shares (small ownership stakes) in the company.

The portion of profit that the company decides to share with its shareholders is called a dividend.

Think of it like this: imagine you and four friends each own 20% of a small bakery. The bakery earns $1,000 in profit this month. You all agree to keep $600 to buy a new oven and distribute the remaining $400 among yourselves. Each person gets $80. That $80 is your dividend — your share of the profit, paid to you simply for being an owner.

How dividends work in practice

In real companies, dividends are paid out per share. So if a company declares a dividend of $2 per share, and you own 50 shares, you receive $100.

Dividends are most commonly paid in cash, deposited directly into the shareholder's brokerage account. However, some companies pay dividends in the form of additional shares of stock instead of cash — this is called a stock dividend.

Most large companies that pay dividends do so on a regular schedule, typically four times a year (quarterly). Some pay monthly, and some pay annually. The key dates to know are:

  • Declaration date — the day the company's board officially announces the dividend and states the amount.
  • Ex-dividend date — a cutoff date. You must own the shares before this date to be entitled to receive the upcoming dividend. If you buy shares on or after this date, you won't receive that particular payout.
  • Record date — the date the company checks its official records to confirm which shareholders qualify.
  • Payment date — the actual day the money lands in shareholders' accounts.

Not all companies pay dividends

Paying a dividend is not a legal obligation — it is entirely the company's choice, decided by its board of directors. Many younger, fast-growing companies (think of startups or technology companies focused on rapid expansion) pay no dividend at all. They reason that keeping all the profit in the business will grow the company faster, which will eventually make each share worth more. Shareholders of such companies profit not through dividends but through the rising price of their shares.

On the other hand, large, stable, mature companies — like utilities, banks, and consumer goods companies — tend to pay regular, reliable dividends. These companies have steady income and don't need to reinvest every dollar to grow.

Dividend yield

A useful related concept is dividend yield. It tells you how much dividend income you earn relative to the price you paid for the shares. It is expressed as a percentage.

For example: if a share costs $100 and the company pays $4 in dividends per year, the dividend yield is 4%. This helps investors compare how "rewarding" different stocks are in terms of income.

Special dividends

Occasionally, a company will pay a special dividend — a one-time, extra payment to shareholders, usually because the company had an unusually profitable period or sold off a major asset. This is separate from its regular dividend schedule.

Dividend reinvestment

Many brokerages offer a Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRIP), where instead of receiving your dividend as cash, it is automatically used to buy more shares of the same company. Over time, this can significantly compound your ownership and returns.

Why dividends matter

For investors, dividends serve as a form of passive income — money you earn simply by holding shares, without selling anything. This is especially valuable for retirees or anyone who wants a steady income stream from their investments. Consistent dividend payments are also often seen as a signal that a company is financially healthy and confident in its future earnings.

In arithmetic, when you perform a division operation, the dividend is the number being divided.

In the expression 12 ÷ 4 = 3:

  • 12 is the dividend (the number being split up)
  • 4 is the divisor (the number you're dividing by)
  • 3 is the quotient (the result)

A simple way to remember it: the dividend is what gets "divided." It's the whole amount you're starting with before you split it into parts.

In general language, dividend is sometimes used loosely to mean a benefit, reward, or positive outcome that results from some earlier effort or decision.

You'll often hear phrases like:

  • "Years of hard training finally paid dividends when she won the championship." — Her earlier hard work produced a rewarding payoff.
  • "The peace dividend" — a well-known phrase used to describe the economic benefits a country gains when a war or conflict ends and it no longer needs to spend so heavily on its military. That freed-up money becomes a kind of "dividend" paid to the nation.

In this figurative sense, think of a dividend as the fruits of something — the positive return you receive on an investment of time, effort, or resources.

ContextWhat "dividend" means
FinanceThe share of a company's profits distributed to its shareholders
MathematicsThe number being divided in a division problem
FigurativeA benefit or reward gained from a prior effort or decision

(Only including this compact summary as a reference — all the substance is in the prose above.)

The financial meaning is by far the most common in adult life. A dividend is simply your cut of the profits, earned by virtue of ownership.
4609:
Divination is the practice of trying to discover hidden knowledge — especially about the future, or about something unknown or secret — through supernatural or mystical means. In other words, it is the act of seeking answers that ordinary human senses and logic cannot provide, by tapping into what believers consider a higher power, cosmic force, or spiritual realm.

Think of it this way: when a person cannot know something through normal means — like what will happen tomorrow, whether a decision will turn out well, or where a lost person is — they might turn to divination. Instead of using science or reason, they use rituals, special objects, signs from nature, or spiritual methods to try to "receive" that hidden knowledge.

The heart of divination rests on a belief: that the universe, the gods, or some greater invisible force already knows everything — past, present, and future — and that this force communicates its knowledge through signs, patterns, and symbols, if only you know how to read them.

A diviner (the person performing divination) is someone who claims to be able to read those signs and translate them into answers.
What Kind of Answers Does Divination Seek?

Divination can be used to seek three broad types of knowledge:

1. Knowledge about the future — Will this harvest be good? Will I be successful in this battle? Will this marriage be happy? This is the most common use.

2. Knowledge about hidden present things — Where is the missing person? Who committed the crime? What is the cause of this illness?

3. Guidance for making decisions — Should I take this path or that one? What does the god/universe want me to do?

There is no single method. Across history and cultures, people have practiced divination in hundreds of ways. Here are some well-known examples:

  • Astrology — Studying the positions of stars and planets to predict a person's fate or future events.
  • Tarot cards — Drawing and interpreting a special deck of illustrated cards to gain insight into a situation.
  • Palmistry — Reading the lines, shapes, and markings on a person's hand to reveal their destiny or personality.
  • Runes — Casting small stones or tiles carved with ancient symbols and interpreting how they fall.
  • Scrying — Gazing into a reflective surface (like a crystal ball, a mirror, or still water) to receive visions.
  • Reading tea leaves — Interpreting the patterns left by tea leaves at the bottom of a cup after drinking.
  • Augury — Watching the flight patterns or behavior of birds and reading them as signs.
  • Dream interpretation — Believing that dreams carry divine or prophetic messages and decoding their meaning.
  • The I Ching — An ancient Chinese system where coins or sticks are thrown and the resulting patterns are matched to passages in a sacred text for guidance.

What all of these have in common is the same underlying act: using something physical or observable as a bridge to access knowledge that is otherwise beyond human reach.
Divination vs. Words You Might Confuse It With

Divination vs. Fortune-telling: Fortune-telling is a casual, everyday term for the same basic activity — predicting the future using mystical means. Divination is the more formal and serious term, often used in historical, religious, or academic contexts. A street fair has a "fortune-teller." A history book discusses "divination practices in ancient Rome."

Divination vs. Prophecy: A prophet receives a direct message from a god or divine force — the knowledge comes to them, often uninvited, like a vision or a voice. A diviner actively seeks that knowledge by performing a ritual and interpreting signs. The prophet is a passive receiver; the diviner is an active seeker.

Divination vs. Magic: Magic usually refers to the act of causing something to happen through supernatural power. Divination is about knowing — not making things happen, but discovering hidden truths. The goal of divination is information, not action.
The Cultural and Historical Weight of the Word

Divination is not a fringe or minor concept — it has been deeply woven into the fabric of nearly every human civilization throughout history. Ancient Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, Chinese, Mesopotamians, Aztecs, Celts, and countless other cultures all practiced some form of it, often treating it as a serious and sacred matter. Roman generals consulted augurs (official diviners) before battles. The ancient Greeks traveled long distances to seek answers from the Oracle at Delphi — a priestess believed to channel divine wisdom. Chinese emperors used oracle bones (animal bones heated until they cracked, with the cracks then read as messages) to make state decisions.

In many ancient societies, divination was not considered superstition — it was considered a genuine and important science, as respected as medicine or law.
How the Word Is Used Today

Today, "divination" is used in several contexts:

  • Historically and academically — to describe the practices of ancient or traditional cultures without judgment. "Divination played a central role in Mesopotamian religious life."
  • In religious or spiritual communities — by people who still practice and believe in these methods seriously.
  • In popular culture — in fantasy novels, films, and games, where divination is a form of magic that lets characters see the future.
  • Loosely and metaphorically — sometimes used humorously to describe any wild guess about the future. "Predicting the stock market sometimes feels like divination."

If you had to remember just one thing: divination is the practice of seeking hidden or future knowledge through supernatural means, by reading signs, omens, or using special rituals — born from the human belief that a greater force knows what we cannot, and that its knowledge can be uncovered if you know how to look.
4610:
When "divine" is used as a noun, it refers to a person of the clergy or a theologian — someone who has dedicated their life to the study, teaching, or practice of religious faith. In plain terms: a priest, a minister, a pastor, or a religious scholar who is deeply learned in theology (the study of God and religious belief).

Think of it this way: just as a native can mean a person who belongs to a place, a divine means a person who belongs to — or serves — the domain of God and religion.

"The divines of the church gathered to settle the dispute over scripture."

Here, "divines" simply means a group of learned clergy or theologians.

This is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. You won't hear it in everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it frequently in historical texts, literature, philosophy, and religious writings — especially from the 16th to 19th centuries. For example, the famous "Westminster Assembly of Divines" (1643) was a gathering of theologians convened to reform the English church.

There is a second, distinct usage of "divine" as a noun — when it appears as "the Divine" (usually capitalized, always with the). Here, it does not refer to a person. Instead, it refers to God, or the quality of being God, or the sacred spiritual power that underlies all existence.

This usage is abstract and philosophical. It captures the idea of the supreme, the holy, the infinite — whatever a person or tradition considers to be the ultimate spiritual reality.

"Artists have long tried to capture the Divine in their work."
"She felt a deep yearning to connect with the Divine."
"Many philosophers have argued about the nature of the Divine."

Notice that in this usage, "the Divine" stands in for something vast and sacred — it is a way of talking about God or ultimate holiness without naming any specific religion or deity. It is often preferred in philosophical, mystical, or interfaith contexts precisely because it is broad and non-sectarian.
Two Distinct Usages, Side by Side

To keep it clear in your mind:

  • "A divine" / "the divines" → a person (a clergyman or theologian). Countable. Old-fashioned.
  • "The Divine" → an abstract idea (God, the sacred, the holy). Uncountable. Still in active use in philosophy, spirituality, and literature.

"A divine" (meaning a clergy member or theologian) appears almost exclusively in:

  • Historical writing and documents
  • Classic English literature (Shakespeare's era through the Victorian era)
  • Academic writing about religion and history

You would not call a modern priest "a divine" in casual speech — it would sound archaic. But if you're reading older texts or writing in a formal, literary style, it fits perfectly.

"The Divine" (meaning God or the sacred) is alive and well today. You'll find it in:

  • Philosophy of religion
  • Mystical and spiritual writing (across many traditions — Christian, Hindu, Sufi, New Age, etc.)
  • Poetry and literary prose
  • Interfaith dialogue, where a neutral term for the sacred is useful

Both uses of "divine" as a noun share the same root idea: something — or someone — connected to God or to the highest spiritual reality. Whether it is a theologian who spends his life studying God ("a divine"), or the infinite sacred presence itself ("the Divine"), the word always carries a sense of the holy, the elevated, and the transcendent.

If you ever see "divine" in a text and you're unsure which meaning applies, ask yourself: Is it referring to a person, or to an abstract spiritual idea? That distinction will always guide you to the right meaning.
4611:
To divine something means to discover or figure out something hidden, unknown, or unclear — not by being told directly, and not through obvious logic, but through a special kind of sensing, intuition, or supernatural power.

Think of it this way: when you know something without anyone explaining it to you, and without a clear, step-by-step reason for knowing it — as if the answer came to you from some invisible source — that is the spirit of divining.

This verb operates on two levels that sit right next to each other. Understanding both will give you the complete picture.

1. The Everyday, Human Level — Intuitive Discovery

In ordinary, modern usage, to divine something means to perceive or figure out something that is not obvious, using sharp intuition or instinct.

It is similar to "sensing" or "guessing," but it is stronger and more accurate than a random guess. The person who divines something arrives at a correct understanding through a kind of deep, almost mysterious inner perception — not through someone handing them the answer.

Examples:

  • "Somehow, she divined exactly what he was feeling, even though he said nothing."
  • "The detective divined the killer's next move before any evidence pointed that way."
  • "He couldn't explain how, but he divined that something was wrong the moment he walked into the room."

Notice that in all these cases, the person knows something they were never explicitly told. There's a gap between the available information and the conclusion — and divining is what bridges that gap.

2. The Supernatural, Ancient Level — Magical or Mystical Discovery

At its deeper, more traditional level, to divine means to use supernatural or mystical means to uncover hidden truths, find hidden things, or predict what will happen in the future.

This is where the word carries a sense of magic, prophecy, and the sacred. Historically, certain people — called diviners — were believed to have special powers to read signs invisible to ordinary people: the flight of birds, the patterns in fire, the stars, or the lines of a palm.

Examples:

  • "The ancient priest claimed to divine the will of the gods from the way the smoke rose."
  • "She divined the future by reading the pattern of tea leaves in the cup."
  • "The shaman was called to divine the location of the missing child."

One very specific and well-known use is water divining (also called dowsing) — the practice of walking across land holding a forked stick, which is believed to bend and point downward when underground water is below. The person doing this is called a water diviner. Whether or not this actually works is debated, but the practice itself is very real and historically widespread.
The Key Quality That Unites Both Meanings

Whether it is intuitive or supernatural, the act of divining always involves:

  • Something that is hidden, unclear, or not directly available
  • A person who reaches through that invisibility to find the truth
  • A method that goes beyond ordinary reasoning or physical evidence

This is what separates divining from simply figuring something out. When you figure something out, you can usually explain the steps you took. When you divine something, the process feels almost inexplicable — as if the knowledge came from somewhere beyond the normal, visible world.
The Related Words You Will Encounter

Understanding the verb is incomplete without knowing its close family:

  • Diviner — a person who divines; someone with the gift or practice of finding hidden truths. "The village diviner was consulted whenever livestock went missing."
  • Divination — the noun for the broader practice or art of divining, especially through supernatural methods. "Ancient civilizations relied heavily on divination before going to war." Divination includes things like reading tarot cards, consulting oracles, astrology, and reading omens.
  • Divined — past tense. "She divined his intentions before he even opened his mouth."
  • Divining — present participle, used for ongoing action. "He spent his life divining the secrets of the universe."
How It Feels — The Tone of the Word

This verb carries a quietly powerful and slightly mysterious tone. It is not a casual word. When a writer uses divine as a verb, they are suggesting that the knowledge gained is special — almost gifted, almost otherworldly. It elevates the act of discovery into something more than ordinary.

If someone says "he guessed what I was thinking," it sounds lucky or coincidental. But if someone says "he divined what I was thinking," it sounds like he reached into something deep and unseen and pulled out the truth — which is a much more striking and impressive image.

To divine is to discover something hidden or unknown — either through a deep, almost supernatural intuition (in everyday use), or through an actual mystical or magical practice (in its traditional sense) — in a way that goes beyond ordinary seeing or reasoning.
4612:
When something is divisive, it causes people to split into opposing sides. It creates sharp disagreement, tension, or conflict — pulling people apart rather than bringing them together.

Think of it like a knife cutting a group of people in half. On one side are those who strongly support something; on the other side are those who strongly oppose it. The thing that caused that split is divisive.

Almost anything can be divisive — a topic, a person, a decision, a policy, a statement, a piece of art, or even a choice made at work. What matters is not what it is, but what it does: it causes people to disagree strongly and take opposing sides.

Politics: A new tax law that some people love and others deeply hate is divisive. It doesn't just create mild disagreement — it creates passionate, opposing camps.

Society: Topics like immigration, gun control, or capital punishment are often called divisive because they reliably split entire populations into strongly opposed groups.

Workplace: A manager who openly favors certain employees over others can be divisive — their behavior creates tension, jealousy, and conflict within the team.

Sports: Imagine a referee makes a questionable call in a big game. Half the fans think it was fair; the other half think it was outrageous. That call was divisive.

Art & Culture: A controversial film, book, or song that causes half the audience to praise it and the other half to condemn it is divisive.
The Key Ingredient: Strong, Opposing Reactions

For something to be truly divisive, the disagreement it creates must be strong. If people have mildly different opinions, we wouldn't usually call it divisive. The word implies a deep, passionate split — often one where both sides feel very strongly and find it hard to meet in the middle.

It also implies that the disagreement is more than just intellectual — it often carries emotion. People don't just think differently; they may feel frustrated, angry, or upset with those on the other side.

Divisive almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When you call something divisive, you are usually suggesting it is harmful or undesirable — that it is tearing a community, country, group, or relationship apart.

For example:

  • "The president's speech was divisive." — This implies the speech caused unnecessary conflict and split people apart, and the speaker probably disapproves of this outcome.
  • "We need to move away from divisive rhetoric." — This means: we need to stop using language that inflames conflict and turns people against each other.

However, the word itself does not make a moral judgment about who is right. It simply describes the effect — that something causes division. Both sides of a divisive debate can be right or wrong; the word only tells you that the split exists and is sharp.

• It does not mean simply "controversial." A controversial thing sparks debate and discussion, but a divisive thing specifically splits people into opposing camps with strong feeling. All divisive things tend to be controversial, but not all controversial things are divisive.
  • It does not mean "difficult" or "complicated." A math problem can be difficult, but not divisive. Divisive is specifically about people being pulled apart.
  • It does not require a 50/50 split. Even if 80% of people support something, if the remaining 20% oppose it passionately and the disagreement creates real tension and conflict, it can still be called divisive.
Who or What Gets Called Divisive

The word is used to describe:

  • Issues/topics — "Abortion is one of the most divisive issues in modern politics."
  • People — "He is a divisive figure — people either admire him greatly or despise him."
  • Actions/decisions — "The company's decision to cut salaries was divisive and damaged team morale."
  • Language/rhetoric — "The politician was criticized for using divisive language that turned communities against each other."
  • Policies — "The new school policy was divisive among parents."

To deepen your understanding, here are words that are close in meaning:

  • Polarizing — very similar; means something pushes people to extreme, opposing positions. (A polarizing figure is one people either love or hate.)
  • Contentious — causing argument and disagreement. Slightly milder than divisive.
  • Inflammatory — something that deliberately stirs up strong emotion and conflict.
  • Controversial — sparking debate and disagreement; broader and milder than divisive.

The opposite of divisive would be words like: unifying, cohesive, inclusive, harmonious — things that bring people together rather than split them apart.
Divisive describes something that causes people to split into strongly opposing sides, creating conflict, tension, and disagreement — and it almost always implies this split is unwanted or harmful.
4613:
Divisiveness is the quality of causing people to split into opposing groups that disagree with, resent, or conflict with each other. When something has divisiveness, it doesn't just create mild disagreement — it drives people apart, breaks unity, and creates tension or hostility between sides.

Think of it this way: imagine a rope being pulled from both ends until it tears in the middle. Divisiveness is the force doing the pulling.

The word comes from the idea of dividing — but not in the harmless math sense. In human terms, to divide people means to push them into separate, opposing camps where they stop seeing themselves as part of the same team.

Divisiveness is the degree to which something has that power — the power to cause that kind of split.

So when someone says, "There is a lot of divisiveness in the country right now," they mean: people in that country are deeply split — they hold strongly opposing views, they feel hostile toward those who disagree with them, and the sense of shared community is weakened or broken.
What Divisiveness Looks Like in Real Life

Divisiveness can appear in many places:

In politics: A politician who constantly portrays one group of citizens as the enemy of another is practicing divisiveness. Their words don't just express an opinion — they actively push people into hostile opposing camps.

In a workplace: A manager who plays employees against each other, shares gossip, or gives preferential treatment in ways that cause resentment is creating divisiveness in the team. People stop cooperating and start competing or distrusting each other.

In a family: A topic like inheritance, religion, or an old grudge can cause divisiveness at a family gathering — turning what should be a warm reunion into a battlefield of tension and sides.

In society: Issues like race, immigration, or religion often carry enormous divisiveness — they are topics that quickly split communities into strongly opposed groups with deep emotional investment on each side.

Divisiveness doesn't appear from nowhere. Common causes include:

  • Extreme or inflammatory language — words designed to provoke outrage and paint the "other side" as evil or dangerous.
  • Unfair treatment — when one group feels it is being treated worse than another, resentment and division grow.
  • Propaganda and misinformation — when people are fed distorted or false information, they develop very different pictures of reality, making it nearly impossible to find common ground.
  • Self-interest — sometimes leaders or groups deliberately stoke divisiveness because it benefits them (e.g., "if people are fighting each other, they won't unite against me").
  • Deep value differences — sometimes divisiveness arises genuinely because people hold fundamentally different beliefs about what is right, fair, or important.

Divisiveness is rarely the end of the story. It tends to produce consequences:

  • Erosion of trust — people stop believing those on the "other side" have good intentions.
  • Breakdown of cooperation — groups that are divided struggle to work together on shared problems.
  • Escalation — divisiveness can grow. What starts as disagreement can become hostility, and hostility can become conflict.
  • Echo chambers — divided people stop talking to each other and only interact with those who already agree with them, making the divide even deeper over time.
An Important Nuance: Not All Disagreement Is Divisiveness

This is a subtle but important distinction that many learners miss.

Disagreement is normal and healthy. People debating ideas, arguing different policies, or expressing opposing views is not, by itself, divisiveness.

Divisiveness is specifically about the tearing apart of a group's unity — usually through hostility, resentment, or the deliberate creation of an "us vs. them" mentality. The key ingredient is not just difference of opinion, but the emotional and social rupture that follows.

So: two scientists debating competing theories passionately = disagreement, not divisiveness.
But: a political leader saying "people who disagree with me are traitors and enemies" = divisiveness.

The difference is whether the conflict breaks relationships, community, and mutual respect, or simply represents a normal exchange of differing views.

Divisiveness is not always all-or-nothing. You can describe its intensity:

  • "A small amount of divisiveness" — some mild splitting, some tension.
  • "Deep divisiveness" — severe splits, strong hostility, a community or nation significantly fractured.
  • "Deliberate divisiveness" — someone is intentionally trying to create division for their own benefit.

Since you're learning, it helps to see the whole family of this word:

FormExample
Divide (verb)Conflict tends to divide communities.
Division (noun)There is a deep division between the two groups.
Divisive (adjective)His speech was deliberately divisive.
Divisiveness (noun — the one you're learning)The divisiveness of the debate shocked everyone.
Divisively (adverb)He spoke divisively, inflaming tensions.

These show the word used naturally, so you can feel how it fits:

  1. The divisiveness of the election tore friendships apart.
  2. The CEO's behavior introduced divisiveness into a team that once worked seamlessly together.
  3. Critics accused the media of spreading divisiveness by sensationalizing every conflict.
  4. Social media algorithms are often blamed for increasing political divisiveness.
  5. The community leader urged people to resist divisiveness and focus on shared goals.
  6. Years of economic inequality had bred a divisiveness that no single speech could heal.
Divisiveness is the quality of splitting people into hostile, opposing groups — breaking down unity, trust, and cooperation — whether through words, actions, policies, or ideas.
4614:
A divot is a small chunk of earth — grass, soil, and roots all stuck together — that gets scooped or torn out of the ground, leaving a little hollow behind. Think of it as a bite taken out of the ground.

The word actually carries two related meanings at once, and this is important:

  • The piece of turf that was removed → that's a divot.
  • The hole or depression left behind after the piece is gone → that's also called a divot.

Both meanings are correct and widely used. Context usually makes clear which one is meant.
Where You'll Hear It Most: Golf

The word is most at home on a golf course, and understanding golf makes the word click instantly.

When a golfer swings a club to hit the ball, the club's sharp edge sometimes digs into the turf and slices out a small, flat flap of grass and dirt. That flap — and the dent it leaves in the ground — is a divot.

Good golf etiquette requires players to "replace their divot," meaning they pick up that torn-out piece and press it back into the hole so the course stays smooth for others. You'll often see golfers carrying a small tool called a "divot repair tool" for this exact purpose.

So on a golf course:

  • "He took a big divot with that iron shot." → His club dug out a noticeable chunk of turf.
  • "The ball rolled right into a divot." → The ball landed in one of those little hollows in the ground.
  • "Please replace your divots." → A polite reminder on course signs.

The word has traveled well beyond golf. In everyday language, a divot refers to any small dent, hollow, or indentation in a surface — not just grass. The logic is the same: something is missing from a surface, leaving a little depression.

Examples:

  • "There's a divot in the drywall where the doorknob hit it." → A small dent in the wall.
  • "The car has a divot on the hood from the hailstorm." → A small rounded dent.
  • "The mattress has a divot in the middle from years of use." → A sunken, worn-down area.
  • "She had a small divot on her chin — a little natural indentation." → A slight hollow in skin.

In all these cases, the image is consistent: a small, localized depression where the surface dips inward or where material is missing.
The Key Qualities of a Divot

To use the word accurately, keep these features in mind:

  • Small in size. A divot is never a large crater or a wide ditch. It's modest — a few inches at most. If the hole is large, people reach for different words (pit, crater, trench, pothole).
  • Relatively shallow. A divot is a surface-level scoop, not a deep hole.
  • Caused by force or pressure. Divots don't form on their own — something digs, hits, or presses into the surface to create one.
  • Localized. A divot is a specific spot, not a general unevenness.

If you had to carry just one image in your head for "divot," let it be this: a golf club swinging down, slicing a little flap of turf out of the green, and leaving a shallow scooped-out hollow in the ground. That image — the missing piece and the depression it leaves — is the heart of the word. Everything else is just that same idea applied to walls, car hoods, mattresses, skin, or any other surface where a small chunk is missing or pushed in.
4615:
To divulge something means to reveal or share information that was previously private, secret, or confidential.

When you divulge something, you are taking information that was being kept hidden — either by you or someone else — and bringing it out into the open by telling someone about it.

Think of it this way: if information is locked inside a vault, divulging it means you opened the vault and let someone see what's inside.
